# What this book establishes {.unnumbered}

This book reports a research program on **surrogates for steady,
boundary-driven, three-dimensional PDE problems**: given a discretized
boundary (a surface mesh with normals and areas) and a few global conditions
such as the freestream direction, predict the fields on that boundary and in
the volume around it. The program built an architecture, ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention; the code class is `ISLA`, formerly `MeshTransformer2`),^[Pronounced "eye-la"; an *isla* is an island, a shape defined entirely by
its boundary. An earlier exact-kernel design of this program is documented in
the repository's `book/archive/` directory, outside this book.] and measured it
against the strongest baseline tested under this protocol, GeoTransolver, under one
frozen, parameter- and token-matched protocol on two production aerodynamics
datasets (DrivAerML, HiLiftAeroML). The
audience is applied mathematicians and machine-learning researchers; every
term is defined at first use and every number is computed live from a
checked-in artifact.

## The verdict {#sec-verdict}

**ISLA is a large improvement over GeoTransolver in one regime, scarce
training data on a family of multi-element wing geometries; elsewhere it
ranges from parity to 1.3x behind, and it is not a new capability.** That
sentence is the whole book, and every chapter either supports one clause of
it or bounds it.

The regime where it wins is practically important. On HiLiftAeroML, with
35 CFD runs, ISLA's surface-pressure error is 2.8x lower than
GeoTransolver's and than plain Transolver's. Read horizontally, the same
curves say GeoTransolver needs about six times as many training cases to
reach the accuracy ISLA reaches from 35, and plain Transolver about twice as
many as ISLA at the 0.09 error level (@sec-de-result). In engineering terms, from 35 CFD runs ISLA predicts lift
and drag coefficients of unseen configurations to about 3%, where the
baselines reach 8–17% (errors against the label integrated on the same
10,000 sampled cells, not against the full-surface force; @sec-de-forces);
at a fixed angle of attack, 126 training geometries give ISLA lift to 0.6%
on the same terms and a 5.0x advantage over GeoTransolver on 18 validation
geometries never seen at any angle. The advantage holds on every one of the
180 shared validation cases at 35 cases, on geometries never seen in
training, and after every
steel-man control constructed for the baselines (higher learning rate,
doubled epochs, a third seed, the same attention family without a geometry
encoder). What ISLA does with few samples is generalize across wing
geometries; GeoTransolver does not turn additional training geometries into
accuracy until it has hundreds of them.

Three facts bound it. The multiplier shrinks with data: 2.2x at 210 cases,
parity at 1,260, and a naive power-law extrapolation of the two curves
favours GeoTransolver by two at 5,000 cases. It does not transfer to
DrivAerML, whose geometries are smooth morphs of one car: there GeoTransolver
is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 training cases up and 8.5% more accurate at
full data, and the ingredient of ISLA that makes the difference between the
two datasets has not been isolated. And part of the 2.8x is GeoTransolver's
weakness rather than ISLA's strength: plain Transolver beats GeoTransolver at
210 cases, so against the strongest same-family baseline ISLA's margin there
is 1.3x.

What ISLA adds beyond accuracy is contracts and cost: rotation and
translation covariance exact by algebraic construction (the finite-precision
residual of the bf16 training path is a measured quantity, @sec-mt2-contracts),
stable training across a decade of learning rate where GeoTransolver degrades
4–14x, and, on one GPU with one instrument, 1.6 GiB of peak training
memory at 10,000 tokens for its current code against GeoTransolver's
4.1 GiB; the ISLA checkpoints behind this book's accuracy numbers were
trained with an earlier version of the code that peaked at 9.3 GiB, and
ISLA's training step is 3.7x slower (@sec-cost). One architecture
covers both tasks: with its interior queries admitted as interacting tokens
and given the signed distance to the wall, ISLA is more accurate than
GeoTransolver's 27.6M-parameter volume configuration on interior pressure
(0.057 against 0.062) and velocity (0.085 against 0.133) at 8.9M parameters,
and less accurate on eddy viscosity (0.122 against 0.094); below full data it
leads on velocity and trails within 6–11% on pressure. The passive,
query-independent interior decode is 2.6x behind on pressure; that is the
cost of the complete passive configuration as built (a separate read
decoder, no signed-distance input), not a measured price of query
independence alone (@sec-interior-results). Where nothing leads is regime
extrapolation: across an
angle-of-attack or stall boundary every architecture tested loses about a
factor of ten, so coverage, not architecture, governs that axis.

| Setting | Standing | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| HiLift surface, 35 cases | ISLA far ahead | 2.8x vs both baselines; 180/180 cases; forces 3% vs 8–17% against sampled-cell label integrals |
| HiLift surface, 210 cases | ISLA ahead | 2.2x vs GeoTransolver, 1.3x vs Transolver |
| HiLift, never-seen geometries (18 validation geometries) | ISLA ahead | 1.4–1.8x mixed angle; 5.0x at a fixed angle |
| HiLift surface, 1,260 cases | Parity | GeoTransolver/ISLA 1.02 |
| DrivAerML surface, 27–435 cars | ISLA behind | GeoTransolver 1.2–1.3x ahead; 8.5% at full data |
| DrivAerML interior, 435 cars | ISLA ahead on pressure, velocity; behind on eddy viscosity; advantage tied to querying ≥10,000 points together | 0.91x / 0.64x / 1.29x at a third of the parameters; pressure error 0.062 → 0.110 when 1,000 points are queried alone |
| DrivAerML interior, 54–109 cars | Mixed | pressure 1.06–1.11x behind, velocity ahead, eddy viscosity 1.45x behind |
| Regime extrapolation | Nobody wins | both lose about 10x |
| Contracts and cost | Mixed | SE(3) covariance by construction; learning-rate robust; memory 1.6 vs 4.1 GiB for the current code, 9.3 GiB as trained; step 3.7x slower |

: The standing of ISLA against GeoTransolver in every setting measured, as
baseline error divided by ISLA error where a ratio is given (above one
favours ISLA). Each row's protocol, seeds, statistics and artifact are in
the chapter that owns it: @sec-data-efficiency (HiLift rows), @sec-full-data
(parity, DrivAerML surface, regime extrapolation, contracts),
@sec-interior (interior rows). {#tbl-verdict}

## The result in one picture

```{python}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML. Surface-pressure relative L2 error on
#|   the shared 180-case validation set versus number of training cases, for
#|   GeoTransolver (red circles), ISLA (blue squares) and plain
#|   Transolver (grey triangles, dashed). Lines join seed means; bands span
#|   the seeds; annotated factors are each baseline's error divided by ISLA's
#|   at the same rung (above one favours ISLA). Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface
#|   points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation, each architecture
#|   at its best learning rate, three seeds at 35 and 210 cases and two at
#|   1,260, final-epoch checkpoints, validation set; the test split is sealed. The full figure, the
#|   paired per-case statistics, the force-coefficient errors and the controls
#|   are in @sec-data-efficiency. It does not show scaling beyond 1,260 cases
#|   (@sec-limits). Data: results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json,
#|   results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json,
#|   results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json (third seeds).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
data = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi = [], [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(a=arch, s=s) in lad]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); lo.append(min(v)); hi.append(max(v))
    data[arch] = (xs, means, lo, hi)
xs, means, lo, hi = [], [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = None
    for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3"):
        v = [t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(lr=lr, s=s) in t1]
        if len(v) >= 2 and (best is None or statistics.mean(v) < statistics.mean(best)):
            best = v
    xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(best)); lo.append(min(best)); hi.append(max(best))
data["t"] = (xs, means, lo, hi)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.8))
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o", "-", 2.2), "t": (GREY, "Transolver", "^", "--", 1.6), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s", "-", 2.2)}
for arch in ("gt", "t", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi = data[arch]; c, name, mk, ls, lw = style[arch]
    ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color=c, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=lw, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("GeoTransolver", (35, data["gt"][1][0]), xytext=(14, 2), textcoords="offset points", color=RED, fontweight="bold", va="center")
ax.annotate("ISLA", (210, data["mt2"][1][1]), xytext=(14, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=BLUE, fontweight="bold", va="center")
xm, ym = (35 * 210) ** 0.5, (data["t"][1][0] * data["t"][1][1]) ** 0.5
ax.annotate("Transolver", (xm, ym), xytext=(-3, -7), textcoords="offset points", color=GREY, fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="top",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
for i, n in enumerate((35, 210)):
    r_gt = data["gt"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]; r_t = data["t"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]
    ymid = (data["gt"][1][i] * data["mt2"][1][i]) ** 0.5
    ax.annotate("", (n, data["mt2"][1][i]), (n, data["gt"][1][i]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=INK2, lw=0.9, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=4))
    ax.text(n * 1.08, ymid, f"GeoTransolver {r_gt:.1f}x ISLA\nTransolver {r_t:.1f}x ISLA", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="center", linespacing=1.3,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
r_full = data["gt"][1][2] / data["mt2"][1][2]
ax.annotate(f"{r_full:.2f}x (parity)", (1260, (data["gt"][1][2] * data["mt2"][1][2]) ** 0.5), xytext=(14, 30), textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260"])
ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"])
ax.set_xlim(22, 3200)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]", color=INK2)
ax.set_title("Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML (shared 180-case validation set)", color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=11, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## How to read this book

Part I defines the problem, the datasets and splits, the metrics and the
protocol (@sec-problem), then the architecture, ISLA
(@sec-mt2), and the baselines with the fair-comparison rules
(@sec-baselines). Part II is the evidence on production aerodynamics: data
efficiency (@sec-data-efficiency); accuracy at full data, the robustness
contracts and regime extrapolation (@sec-full-data,
@sec-regime-extrapolation); and boundary-to-interior prediction
(@sec-interior), which also answers why the architecture does not evaluate
exact boundary-integral kernels (@sec-interior-negatives). Part III
states the limits of every claim and the experiments that would move them
(@sec-limits) and holds the live status ledger of the program
(@sec-program-status). The appendix is the dated lab notebook
(@sec-notebook): every preregistration, launch and verdict, including the
failed ones, in the order they happened.

Three habits of this book: a comparison is only reported when parameters,
tokens per case, epochs and peak memory are matched or the mismatch is
stated in the same sentence, and every ratio between architectures is written
as baseline error divided by ISLA error, so a value above one favours ISLA; a claim is only reported with the split it was
measured on and the statistic behind it; and a limit is stated next to the
claim it limits, not in a separate place.

## What this book does not claim

ISLA's data-efficiency advantage is a statement about 35 to 1,260 training
cases on HiLiftAeroML; on DrivAerML, at the frozen learning rate, GeoTransolver
is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 cases up and the two tie at 14. ISLA's curve
flattens where GeoTransolver's steepens: a naive power-law extrapolation of the
two curves puts GeoTransolver at 0.015 and ISLA at 0.029 at 5,000 cases, a
factor of two in GeoTransolver's favour (@sec-limits). The 2.8x headline is
against GeoTransolver and plain Transolver at 35 cases; at 210 cases the
margin over plain Transolver, the stronger baseline there, is 1.3x. The
HiLift accuracy figures are validation-set figures (final-epoch checkpoints,
no checkpoint selection; the sealed test was spent on regime extrapolation,
and because those regime test sets cover all 180 geometries, every remaining
HiLiftAeroML split is held out per checkpoint but is not an independent
program-level confirmation, @sec-limits-validation). The advantage is
geometry generalization — at a fixed angle of attack on 18 validation
geometries never seen at any angle ISLA is 5.0x more accurate than
GeoTransolver — but the ingredient that carries it is not identified: no
single ISLA ingredient accounts for more than 16% of it; the baselines
receive the freestream as a physical velocity (2,679.5 in/s on
HiLiftAeroML) where ISLA receives a unit direction, a conditioning
difference whose effect on the trained gap is not yet measured
(@sec-part-baseline); and the one hypothesis that would explain both
datasets at once (that the advantage lives on the small-scale features of
multi-element wings, the slat and flap gaps) is stated and not yet measured
(@sec-mechanism). ISLA's exact equivariance is a contract, not an
in-distribution accuracy edge on vehicle data: GeoTransolver trained in a
canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at 1% cost (@sec-pose). Its
sampling-density robustness belongs to a configuration (the similarity
gauge) that produced no accuracy number in this book
(@sec-robustness-density). Neither architecture generalizes across a
flow-regime boundary, and neither transfers zero-shot to a different vehicle
family (@sec-regime-extrapolation, @sec-full-data).
